newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea ruling party to elect presidential nominee.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea ruling party to elect presidential nominee.

text.p: South Korea's embattled ruling party holds a national convention on Monday to elect its presidential candidate, with President Kim Young-sam reduced to a lame duck by bribery scandals and political blunders.

Kim, who cannot seek re-election under the constitution, has given up his earlier plan to act as a kingmaker and said he will remain neutral in the first ever open race for a presidential nominee by the country's ruling party.
In the past, ruling party candidates have always won presidential races. The vote for the office is due in December.

Former supreme court judge Lee Hoi-chang has been leading in most public polls among the New Korea Party's six presidential hopefuls but lacks the 50 percent support among party delegates needed to win nomination.
Political analysts said on Sunday he faced tough challenges from Governor Rhee In-je of Kyonggi Province which surrounds Seoul, and ex-premier and legal scholar Lee Soo-sung.
If no one secures 50 percent of votes cast on Monday, a second round of polls would be held later in the day between the first two top contenders.

Kim, who also heads the party, appointed Lee Hoi-chang as party chairman in March in a bid to restore the ruling camp's tarnished image following a series of scandals involving party members and the president's son.
Lee Hoi-chang, who built up his reputation as "Mr Clean" as a supreme court judge, stood down as party chairman earlier this month shortly before registering his candidacy.

Analysts said Kim loyalists would try to install Kim's protege in office to protect him from possible prosecution after retirement. The opposition has suggested they might seek prosecution of the president once he ends his five-year term next February.

The opposition accuses Kim of illegally using money from the scandal-ridden Hanbo Group to fund his presidential campaign in 1992 and of dipping into a slush fund amassed by his disgraced predecessor Roh Tae-woo, who is now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.

A party faction loyal to Kim has made clear it would campaign against Lee Hoi-chang who won prominence after he stood down as premier following a policy row with Kim in 1993. Governor Rhee and Lee Soo-sung have always toed Kim's line.

"Lee Hoi-chang is the front-runner but he faces an uphill battle," said Choi Jang-jip, political science professor at Korea University. "Kim loyalists could rally behind a Kim protege in the runoff poll."

Kim abandoned a plan to name his preferred successor after he took a beating from political blunders. His party provoked almost four weeks of labour strikes after ramming a controversial new labour law through parliament last December.
Several senior party figures are also serving jail terms for taking kickbacks from the Hanbo Group, whose steelmaking flagship collapsed in January, revealing a web of corruption.
Analysts said most worrying for the New Korea Party is the prospect of one of the contenders quitting the party to run alone in December elections. They have been embroiled in mud-slinging recently.
"A split ruling party ticket would give the opposition a chance of victory in December," said Shin Myung-soon, who lectures politics at Yonsei University in Seoul.
Two main opposition parties have already chosen their candidates and the two -- Kim Dae-jung and Kim Jong-pil -- are now negotiating on a single candidacy.
The other three ruling party hopefuls are President Kim's long-time aide Kim Deog-ryong, prosecutor-turned-lawmaker Lee Han-dong and former Seoul mayor Choe Byung-yul.
